steps.title: Find the real change
steps.narration: The submarine rises twenty metres, so its real depth decreases by twenty metres.

steps.title: Scale the change
steps.narration: Apparent depth is real depth divided by the refractive index. Divide the change by four thirds.

steps.title: Read the result
steps.narration: The apparent depth decreases by fifteen metres.

teach.title: Relate the two depths
teach.narration: For an observer looking nearly straight down from air into water, the submarine appears shallower than it really is.

teach.title: Find the first apparent depth
teach.narration: At eighty metres of real depth, multiply by three quarters to get an apparent depth of sixty metres.

teach.title: Find the second apparent depth
teach.narration: At sixty metres of real depth, the same factor gives forty-five metres.

teach.title: Compare the readings
teach.narration: Subtract the second apparent depth from the first. The decrease is fifteen metres.

steps.title: Read the mercury levels
steps.narration: The mercury stands three point five centimetres higher in the arm open to the air.

steps.title: Choose the pressure difference
steps.narration: The gas pushes the mercury down on its own side, so its pressure is higher than atmospheric pressure.

steps.title: Find the gas pressure
steps.narration: Add three point five to seventy-six point zero to get seventy-nine point five centimetres of mercury.

teach.display: Compare at the gas-side mercury level
teach.title: Compare at the same height
teach.narration: Imagine a horizontal line across both arms at the lower mercury surface. The pressures in the connected mercury match at that height.

teach.tag: trace down from the open surface
teach.title: Trace down from the open surface
teach.narration: The open surface is under atmospheric pressure. At the comparison line, the extra column of mercury adds three point five centimetres of mercury to that pressure.

teach.title: Match the gas pressure
teach.narration: At the lower surface on the gas side, the pressure is the pressure of the gas touching it.

teach.title: Add the readings
teach.narration: The gas pressure is seventy-nine point five centimetres of mercury.

steps.title: Convert to base units
steps.narration: Convert eight millihenries and five microfarads to henries and farads.

steps.title: Find the square root
steps.narration: Multiply the inductance and capacitance, then take the square root.

steps.title: Calculate resonance
steps.narration: Divide one by two pi times the square root. The frequency is two thousand five hundred over pi hertz.

teach.title: Identify resonance
teach.narration: At resonance the inductor and capacitor have equal reactance. The resistance in the circuit does not enter this condition.

teach.title: Set up the formula
teach.narration: Equating the two reactances gives one over two pi times the square root of inductance times capacitance.

teach.title: Convert and multiply
teach.narration: Milli means a thousandth and micro means a millionth. After conversion the product is four times ten to the minus eight seconds squared.

teach.title: Take the square root
teach.narration: The square root of four is two, and the exponent of ten halves from minus eight to minus four.

teach.title: Find the frequency
teach.narration: Substitute into the resonance formula and keep two pi in the denominator.

steps.title: Find the lever arms
steps.narration: Measure each distance from the fulcrum at fifteen centimetres. The rod's weight acts at the twenty-five centimetre mark.

steps.title: Balance the moments
steps.narration: The two clockwise moments balance the anticlockwise moment.

steps.title: Solve for the weight
steps.narration: Subtract twelve hundred from two thousand and divide by ten. The weight is eighty newtons.

teach.title: Locate the rod's weight
teach.narration: Treat the rod as uniform, so its weight acts at the midpoint of its fifty-centimetre length.

teach.title: Find the anticlockwise moment
teach.narration: The two hundred newton force is ten centimetres left of the fulcrum. Its downward pull turns the rod anticlockwise.

teach.title: Find the clockwise moments
teach.narration: The rod's weight is ten centimetres right of the fulcrum and the forty newton force is thirty centimetres right. Both produce clockwise moments.

teach.title: Balance about the fulcrum
teach.narration: The rod stays horizontal in equilibrium. The fulcrum's own force has zero lever arm, so the clockwise and anticlockwise moments must balance.

teach.title: Isolate the weight
teach.narration: Subtract twelve hundred and divide by ten centimetres. The weight is eighty newtons, so choose D.

steps.title: Find the frequency
steps.narration: Thirty cycles in six seconds gives five cycles per second.

steps.title: Convert cycles to radians
steps.narration: Each full cycle covers two pi radians around the circle.

steps.title: Find the angular velocity
steps.narration: Five cycles each second gives ten pi radians per second.

teach.title: Count cycles per second
teach.narration: Frequency tells us how many complete cycles happen each second. Divide the cycle count by the time for those cycles.

teach.tag: use the given count and time
teach.title: Use the given count and time
teach.narration: The particle completes thirty cycles in six seconds, so it completes five cycles per second.

teach.title: Convert one cycle
teach.narration: Angular velocity measures angle swept per second. One trip around the circle sweeps two pi radians.

teach.title: Combine the two rates
teach.narration: Multiply five cycles per second by two pi radians per cycle. The result is ten pi radians per second.

steps.title: Use the magnification
steps.narration: Using positive distances for the real object and real image, the image distance is four times the object distance.

steps.title: Substitute into the lens equation
steps.narration: Put four times the object distance in place of the image distance. The focal length is twelve centimetres.

steps.title: Solve for the distance
steps.narration: Combine the fractions and cross multiply. Four times the object distance is sixty centimetres, so the object is fifteen centimetres away.

teach.title: Link image size and distance
teach.narration: Take magnification as a size ratio. With both distances measured as positive lengths, the real image is four times as far from the lens as the object.

teach.title: Write the thin lens equation
teach.narration: The reciprocals of the object distance and image distance add up to the reciprocal of the focal length.

teach.title: Combine the fractions
teach.narration: Replace the image distance with four times the object distance. Rewrite both fractions on the left with a common denominator.

teach.title: Find the object distance
teach.narration: Cross multiply and divide by four. Place the object fifteen centimetres from the lens.

teach.title: Check the placement
teach.narration: Fifteen centimetres is between one and two focal lengths, which gives the real, enlarged image.

steps.title: Convert the time
steps.narration: Two hours is seven thousand two hundred seconds.

steps.title: Find the charge
steps.narration: Multiply the current by the time in seconds for the total charge.

steps.title: Calculate the deposit
steps.narration: Multiply by the mass deposited per coulomb. Rounded to two significant figures this is nine point five times ten to the minus three kilograms.

teach.title: Read the electrochemical equivalent
teach.narration: The electrochemical equivalent tells you how many kilograms of copper are deposited by one coulomb of charge.

teach.title: Convert hours to seconds
teach.narration: An ampere is one coulomb per second, so convert the two hours to seconds before finding the charge.

teach.title: Find the charge passed
teach.narration: Four coulombs pass every second. Over seven thousand two hundred seconds, that gives twenty-eight thousand eight hundred coulombs.

teach.title: Calculate copper mass
teach.narration: Multiply the charge by the copper deposited per coulomb. The coulomb units cancel and leave kilograms.

teach.title: Match the option
teach.narration: Round the result to match the precision of the given electrochemical equivalent.

steps.title: Find the true weight
steps.narration: Multiply the object's two kilograms by ten newtons per kilogram.

steps.title: Find the upthrust
steps.narration: The upthrust equals the weight of the displaced liquid, which is ten newtons.

steps.title: Find the apparent weight
steps.narration: Subtract the upward buoyant force from the downward weight.

teach.title: Find the displaced volume
teach.narration: The object is fully submerged, so it displaces one cubic metre of liquid.

teach.title: Find the displaced mass
teach.narration: Multiply the liquid density by the volume displaced. That amount of liquid has a mass of one kilogram.

teach.title: Find the upward force
teach.narration: Archimedes' principle says the upward force equals the displaced liquid's weight, which is ten newtons.

teach.title: Compare with the true weight
teach.narration: The object's own mass is two kilograms, so gravity pulls it downward with twenty newtons.

teach.title: Subtract the two forces
teach.narration: Ten newtons of upward force offsets part of the twenty newton weight. The apparent weight is ten newtons.

steps.title: Find the resistance rise
steps.narration: The resistance has risen by three ohms from the zero degree reading.

steps.tag: find the fraction of the span
steps.title: Find the fraction of the span
steps.narration: The full span is five ohms, so the reading is six tenths of the way across it.

steps.title: Scale to degrees
steps.narration: The thermometer is linear, so six tenths of a hundred Celsius degrees is sixty degrees Celsius.

teach.tag: use the ice point as zero
teach.title: Use the ice point as zero
teach.narration: This thermometer has a resistance of three ohms at zero degrees Celsius. Measure the rise from that reading.

teach.title: Find the full calibration span
teach.narration: A rise of five ohms corresponds to the full one hundred degree interval.

teach.tag: find the rise at the test point
teach.title: Find the rise at the test point
teach.narration: The test reading is three ohms above the ice-point reading.

teach.title: Interpolate on the linear scale
teach.narration: Three fifths of the resistance span corresponds to three fifths of the temperature span. The temperature is sixty degrees Celsius.

steps.title: Express mass using surface gravity
steps.narration: Rearrange the surface gravity equation to express mass in terms of surface gravity and radius.

steps.title: Insert the Moon-to-Earth ratios
steps.narration: Using the numbers in the question, lunar gravity is one eightieth of Earth's and the Moon's radius is one quarter of Earth's.

steps.title: Simplify the mass ratio
steps.narration: Squaring one quarter gives one sixteenth. The Moon-to-Earth mass ratio is one to one thousand two hundred and eighty.

teach.title: Use the surface gravity formula
teach.narration: Surface gravity increases with mass and decreases with the square of the radius.

teach.title: Write a ratio of masses
teach.narration: Rearrange for mass and divide lunar mass by Earth's mass. The same gravitational constant appears in both formulas and cancels.

teach.title: Put the Moon first
teach.narration: Use the values stated in the question and take size as radius. Put the smaller quantity first in each ratio.

teach.title: Square and multiply
teach.narration: Square the radius ratio before multiplying by the surface gravity ratio. The mass ratio is one to one thousand two hundred and eighty.
